findings.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a record.save inside user validation and ignores its return value, so failed saves (e.g. concurrent-update races on match_count) silently skip the stat update while the email is still correctly blocked. Under concurrent signups of the same blocked email, last_match_at/match_count silently stop being accurate with no error surfaced; operators relying on last_match_at for triage see stale data.

[ADVISORY] The validator issues a synchronous DB read plus a conditional DB write (via BlockedEmail.should_block?) on every user save where email_changed?, turning a previously in-memory validation into a hot-path DB round trip. Every signup and every email change pays two extra DB operations inside validation; a slow or locked blocked_emails table now stalls user creation.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? matches emails case-sensitively, so an admin-blocked 'spam@x.com' does not block 'SPAM@x.com'. A user signing up with a differently-cased variant of a blocked address passes should_block? (where(email: email) is an exact-match query and the email is not downcased), so the block is silently bypassed; the admin must block every case permutation to get coverage.

[ADVISORY] should_block? performs a non-atomic read-modify-write (load record, increment match_count in Ruby, record.save) inside a validation path, so concurrent signups lose increments, and the save's return value is ignored so a failed save silently drops stats. Under concurrent registrations match_count undercounts and last_match_at can be stale; since this runs on every user save with a changed email (hot path through User validation), a failed save due to a concurrent unique-index violation on the same row also silently discards the stat update with no log.

[BUG] The EmailValidator spec stubs should_block? and never exercises the whitelist/blacklist domain-restriction branches that this diff moved out of User#email_validator into EmailValidator#validate_each. The migrated email_domains_whitelist/email_domains_blacklist logic (lib/validators/email_validator.rb lines 6-13), including the Regexp-building helper, ships with zero coverage — a regression there (e.g. the unescaped-domain regex build) would silently disable the site's domain restriction feature with no failing test, and the 'not_allowed' message path is never asserted.

[BUG] No code path in this diff can ever create a BlockedEmail record — there is no admin controller, route, rake task, seed, or UI writer for the new table. The feature is inert in production: operators cannot populate blocked_emails (ActiveRecord-only creation exists in specs via the fabricator), so should_block? always returns false and the entire blocked-email mechanism — model, migration, client rejectedEmails handling — has no reachable effect until someone hand-inserts rows via the database console.

[ADVISORY] The client-side rejectedEmails check compares the raw entered string, so a re-submission with different casing or surrounding whitespace of the same rejected email bypasses the pre-submit check. The user gets the server round-trip and generic failure flash instead of the inline 'invalid' message the client check exists to provide; minor UX gap, not a correctness hole since the server still rejects.

[ADVISORY] The new errors/values JSON payload on the create failure path has no test coverage in this diff, and it serializes user.errors.to_hash for every failed signup including non-email errors. No spec in the diff asserts the shape the client depends on (result.errors.email present and result.values.email populated); a refactor renaming either key breaks the rejectedEmails feedback loop silently, degrading the signup error message back to the generic flash with no failing test.

[BUG] The new validates :email, email: true resolves to the new lib/validators/email_validator.rb (Rails resolves the :email option to the constant EmailValidator), which performs domain whitelist/blacklist and blocked-email checks, not format validation — so basic email format validation is silently dropped, and every email-changed save now runs a DB lookup (BlockedEmail.should_block?) as a validation side effect. Any string passes format validation (e.g. 'not-an-email' is accepted unless domain lists catch it), and every user save with a changed email triggers an UPDATE on blocked_emails, corrupting match_count/last_match_at statistics with non-registration events.

[BUG] The BlockedEmails table has no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin controller, API, rake task, seed, or UI path creates records, so the entire blocklist feature is unreachable and unenforceable in practice. Operators cannot add a blocked email by any supported means; the shipped table, model, validator branch, and i18n string are dead weight until someone hand-inserts rows, and 'comprehensive email validation for blocked users' is not actually delivered to any user.

[BUG] The signup error response now echoes user.errors.to_hash and the submitted name/username/email back to any anonymous client, untraceable to the stated blocked-email requirement. Unrelated scope expansion of a public unauthenticated endpoint: anonymous attackers can use the structured errors/values payload to enumerate which emails are on the blocklist (distinct 'blocked' message vs 'not_allowed' message) and to probe username/email uniqueness rules, with no requirement in this PR calling for it.

[ADVISORY] The rejectedEmails client-side mechanism is not traceable to a blocked-email requirement: it caches the email on ANY email validation failure and then suppresses revalidation with a generic 'invalid' message, conflating server-side blocking with generic client validation state. A user who fixes a typo elsewhere and resubmits the same blocked email gets the generic user.email.invalid message instead of the specific blocked/not_allowed reason the server returned, and the rejectedEmails array lives for the controller lifetime with no reset path, so a transient server error permanently marks an email invalid for the session; reviewers cannot tell from the diff which requirement this client state serves.

[ADVISORY] should_block? mutates and saves statistics (match_count, last_match_at) from inside a read-path validator with no stated requirement for tracking, and the :do_nothing action still increments the counters and hits the DB on every check. Statistics churn is triggered by anyone probing signups (including with do_nothing records, giving attackers a write oracle), and a concurrent save under the unique-email constraint can raise out of validation, turning a signup check into a 500 — none of this behavior is demanded by the PR's stated intent.

[ADVISORY] The new validator's spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? entirely and only exercises the blocked branch, leaving the migrated whitelist/blacklist logic (previously exercised via User#email_validator) without any coverage in this diff. The relocation of domain restriction logic from app/models/user.rb into the validator class is behavior-bearing but unverifiable: a regression in email_in_restriction_setting? or the whitelist-takes-precedence branch ships undetected, and the domain logic is now duplicated in coverage obligation with no test owner.

[BUG] should_block? performs a read-modify-write on match_count (record.match_count += 1; record.save) with no atomic increment or row lock, so concurrent signup attempts against the same blocked email lose counter updates. Two simultaneous requests both read match_count=N and both write N+1; the counter permanently undercounts, corrupting the stats the feature exists to collect. Fix is an atomic UPDATE blocked_emails SET match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ? WHERE email = ?

[BUG] should_block? looks up the blocked email with an exact case-sensitive where(email: email), while email input casing is user-controlled, so 'Spam@x.com' misses a row stored as 'spam@x.com' and the block is bypassed. An attacker trivially defeats the blocklist by varying letter case, and admin-entered blocked emails silently fail to block; the write path (User#email validated downcased elsewhere) and this read path disagree on canonical form.

[BUG] validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which performs a database write (match_count increment + save) inside model validation, so every email validation — not just account creation — mutates the blocked_emails table, and a failed save (e.g. concurrent unique-index violation) silently no-ops with no error handling. Validation becomes a hot write path: any code path that revalidates a user's email (admin edits, email change flows) bumps match_count even when no blocking decision was requested, inflating the metric; the concurrency-induced save failure is swallowed, also skipping the increment inconsistently.

[ADVISORY] The client records the rejected email verbatim from result.values.email and compares it with case-sensitive contains() against the raw accountEmail input, so server-normalized or case-varied retries (e.g. user retypes 'Bob@X.com' after 'bob@x.com' was rejected) bypass the client-side rejectedEmails fast path and re-submit to the server. The UX guard the diff adds only fires on exact-string re-entry; users get the full round-trip error again, and the rejectedEmails array grows unboundedly within the modal session with duplicate/case variants of the same address.

[ADVISORY] The error response now echoes user.attributes.slice('name','username','email') and a raw errors hash back to the client, coupling the JSON contract to User column names with no versioning — any rename or reshaping of user attributes silently changes the public signup-failure payload the new client code depends on. Client and server now co-evolve on an undocumented envelope (result.errors.email / result.values.email); a server-side attribute rename breaks the client-side rejection tracking with no compile-time or contract signal.

[ADVISORY] action_type is stored as a bare integer backed by an in-code Enum with no CHECK constraint or lookup semantics, and the table hardcodes a per-email block model — extending to per-domain or per-pattern blocking (the natural next step for a blocklist) requires a schema migration rather than a data change. Admins must add one row per exact email address; the magic integer column admits any value outside the Enum's two actions, and the schema shape bakes in the exact-match single-address rule.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? compares emails with exact case-sensitive equality and no normalization, so a blocked address is bypassed by any case variant or surrounding whitespace. An admin blocks 'spam@spamclub.com'; a registrant signs up with 'SPAM@spamclub.com' and User.where email lookup misses the record, so the block silently does not apply — the feature's core intent (block a specific email) fails for trivially mutated input. The uniqueness validation on User is likewise default (case-sensitive here), so the drift between 'blocked' and 'enforced' widens.

[BUG] Once an email is pushed into rejectedEmails, the client-side emailValid computation permanently reports 'invalid' for that address for the rest of the modal session, with no mechanism to re-check against the server. If the operator removes the block (or the first failure was transient), the user cannot re-submit the same address without closing and reopening the dialog; submitDisabled keeps the form disabled based on a cached server verdict that is never refreshed — the feedback shown ('invalid') also contradicts the actual server reason ('blocked'), which is a second drift between the server's error taxonomy and the client's displayed message.

[BUG] should_block? increments match_count and writes to the database during model validation, and does so under a read-modify-write race with no locking or atomic update. Every concurrent signup attempt with a blocked email does SELECT then UPDATE; concurrent requests lose increments (match_count undercounts) and, more importantly, user validation now performs a write side effect — a validation pass can fail with a DB error on a record being validated for an unrelated reason, turning a pure check into a mutating operation. An unauthenticated user can also drive writes to blocked_emails on every signup attempt, making the table a write-amplification target.

[ADVISORY] should_block? is an instance-lookup plus mutation helper implemented as a class method with a hidden write side effect, and record.save's return value is ignored. The next maintainer calling should_block? in any read context (admin UI preview, API serialization) silently mutates statistics; a save failure (validation/DB) is swallowed, so match data silently diverges from real attempts. Staff-level concern: this couples 'is it blocked' with 'record the hit' and will be reused incorrectly.

[ADVISORY] The blocked-email check is only reached when the domain whitelist/blacklist checks produce no errors, and the validator runs only if: :email_changed? — blocked-list enforcement is skipped for existing users whose email is unchanged on save and silently bypassed whenever a domain rule already errors. Behavioral asymmetry: a blocked email that also matches the blacklist gets the 'not_allowed' message instead of the blocked one (harmless), but the if: :email_changed? gating means the block list is never consulted for existing accounts, so an admin block only affects new signups/changes — an unstated narrowing of the feature's intent that no test covers.

[ADVISORY] The only spec for the new validator stubs out BlockedEmail.should_block? entirely, so the integration path actually shipped in User (email: true validator wired against SiteSetting whitelist/blacklist plus the real BlockedEmail lookup) is untested. The domain-whitelist/blacklist behavior moved from User#email_validator into EmailValidator is exercised by zero tests in this diff; a regression in the copied gsub/regexp logic or the should_block? integration would pass CI. The stubbed tests also assert only on the stub, verifying nothing about validate_each's real logic.

[ADVISORY] The client keys off result.errors.email truthiness but pushes result.values.email; if the server returns errors without a values payload (older API responses, plugin-rendered errors) the pushObject silently stores undefined. rejectedEmails gains an undefined entry; Em.A.contains(undefined) then never matches a real email, so this is latent today but breaks the moment another server error path includes errors.email without values — a producer/consumer contract split across files with no shared definition of the payload shape.

[BUG] The whitelist/blacklist regex `@(#{domains})` is unanchored, so an email like `attacker@good.com.evil.com` matches the whitelist entry `good.com` and passes the whitelist check while actually resolving at the attacker-controlled domain `evil.com`. An attacker registers with a whitelist-spoofing domain address, defeating the admin's email-domain restriction (the same unanchored match also lets blacklist bypasses like a subdomain-free variant be engineered); the old User#email_in_restriction_setting? carried the same flaw but this diff re-commits it in the new validator that now governs all email changes.

[BUG] should_block? performs an exact-match `where(email: email)` lookup with no case normalization, so `Block@SpamFromHome.org` or any mixed-case variant of a blocked address is not found and is not blocked. Unless every caller downcases before validation (no normalization is added anywhere in this diff), an attacker registers with a case-variant of any blocked email, defeating the block list; the match_count statistic also silently diverges across case variants.

[ADVISORY] The signup failure response now echoes `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values` including the submitted email, turning the unauthenticated /users endpoint into an oracle for probing the admin's blocked-email list and distinguishing 'blocked email' rejections from other validation failures. An unauthenticated attacker can enumerate which specific email addresses the site operators have blocked (and confirm whether a given address was the reason a signup failed), leaking moderation configuration that was previously not exposed per-address.

[ADVISORY] should_block? performs a read-modify-write (`match_count += 1` then `save`) inside the signup validation path with no locking or uniqueness retry, and it fires for every signup attempt with a matching address. Concurrent signup attempts with a blocked email race on the counter update (lost updates), and an unauthenticated attacker can drive unbounded writes to the blocked_emails row by repeatedly submitting the blocked address; under contention the `record.save` can also raise and abort the signup with a 500 instead of a clean validation error.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table is created but this diff ships no writer anywhere (no admin UI, API, rake task, or seed path), so the block list cannot be populated or its action_type toggled by operators. Operators cannot actually use the feature this PR adds: BlockedEmail rows stay empty and should_block? always returns false, making the shipped validator branch and client-side rejectedEmails machinery inert until a separate admin surface lands.

[BUG] Both tests stub BlockedEmail.should_block? with canned return values, so the spec exercises only the validator's if-branch against a mock and never the real BlockedEmail lookup the feature depends on. A regression in BlockedEmail.should_block? (e.g. the record.save failure path, the action_type comparison, or the where(email:) lookup being broken by casing/collation) leaves both tests green because should_block? is stubbed false/true and the real model code is never run inside validation; the spec gives false confidence that blocked emails are actually rejected end-to-end.

[ADVISORY] The domain whitelist/blacklist logic relocated from app/models/user.rb into lib/validators/email_validator.rb has zero test coverage in this diff — the spec only covers the blocked-email branch and never asserts that a whitelist/blacklist violation adds the 'not_allowed' error. The most error-prone code in the moved block (the '.'->'\.' gsub and case-insensitive Regexp.new construction) is unverified: a typo or regexp regression silently disables or inverts domain restriction, and no test in this diff fails. Checked spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb, spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb — neither touches the restriction-setting path.

[ADVISORY] The test named "doesn't add an error when email doesn't match a blocked email" tests the negative case via a stub rather than a real non-blocked record, mirroring the implementation's branch instead of the spec (stub false → assert no error is the trivially-true half of the branch). The test cannot detect a regression where the validator adds a 'blocked' error even when should_block? returns false (e.g. a misplaced errors.add outside the if) — the assertion holds only because the stub path happens to skip the add; a data-driven case (a real BlockedEmail row with action_type :do_nothing) would catch both this validator branch and the real lookup at once.

[ADVISORY] The migration enforces action_type NOT NULL with no DEFAULT, while the default lives only in the BlockedEmail model's before_validation callback, so any row created outside the AR model (seed, admin console, future backfill SQL) raises a NOT NULL violation. Operators seeding or mass-inserting blocked emails via SQL/console get an insert failure on action_type; the schema-level contract diverges from the model-level default.

[ADVISORY] should_block? performs a state-mutating write (match_count increment + last_match_at update) inside the email validation path and ignores the result of record.save, so failed stat writes are silently swallowed. Every signup attempt with a changed email triggers an UPDATE on blocked_emails from an unauthenticated request path; if the save fails (validation or contention) the match statistic is silently lost with no log, and because validation now has a side effect, retrying a signup that fails some other validation double-increments match_count, so the admin-facing statistic counts validation attempts, not actually blocked registrations.

[ADVISORY] match_count is updated via read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1 then save) rather than an atomic increment, so concurrent signups interleave and lose increments. Two simultaneous registrations matching the same blocked email both read the same match_count and one UPDATE overwrites the other, permanently undercounting matches; the correct `increment_counter`/`update_column(match_count: match_count + 1)` form was available.

[ADVISORY] The blocked-email lookup `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` is an exact case-sensitive match while the domain blacklist/whitelist regexp in the same validator is case-insensitive, so case variants of a blocked address silently pass the block. An admin blocks 'spam@foo.com' but a registrant signing up as 'Spam@foo.com' or 'SPAM@FOO.COM' is not blocked and account creation succeeds, defeating the feature for the trivially reachable case-variant bypass.

[ADVISORY] The client pushes the email into rejectedEmails whenever any result.errors.email is present, including 'has already been taken', and email_valid then renders the generic 'invalid' message for an email that is actually taken. A user whose email fails uniqueness sees the inline validation claim the address is invalid while the real reason (taken) is only in the transient flash, misdirecting debugging and user comprehension; the rejectedEmails list is also never cleared on success or modal reopen, so the stale entry persists for the controller's lifetime.

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `BlockedEmail` (model + migration) and wires it into `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?`) plus client-side caching of rejected emails, but it does not add any admin UI/controller/route/task/seed to create/populate `blocked_emails`. In production the mechanism only has effect if rows are inserted out-of-band (e.g., rails/db console), so the feature is operationally incomplete but not a direct correctness bug in the shown code paths.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a client-side pre-submit check `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` where `email` is taken verbatim from `this.get("accountEmail")`, and rejected values are stored via `pushObject(result.values.email)` (from `user.attributes.slice("...","email")`). There is no normalization (trim/downcase) on either side shown in the diff, so string-equality matching can miss the “same” email entered with different casing or surrounding whitespace, causing the intended inline validation to not trigger and requiring another server round-trip. This is a UX/edge-case issue, not a correctness hole because server-side validation still runs.

The added specs cover `EmailValidator` and `BlockedEmail`, but there is no spec in this diff asserting the controller response keys/shape the client relies on, so a future rename/removal of `errors`/`values` or nesting could silently break the rejectedEmails feedback loop without a failing test. This is a concrete, diff-grounded test/contract gap rather than a current functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new validates :email, email: true resolves to the new lib/validators/email_validator.rb (Rails resolves the :email option to the constant EmailValidator), which performs domain whitelist/blacklist and blocked-email checks, not format validation — so basic email format validation is silently dropped, and every email-changed save now runs a DB lookup (BlockedEmail.should_block?) as a validation side effect. adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `User` changed to `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` and a new `lib/validators/email_validator.rb` defines `EmailValidator`, so `email: true` will indeed invoke this custom validator. That validator performs only domain whitelist/blacklist checks and then calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, which does a DB query and, if a matching `BlockedEmail` exists, increments `match_count`/updates `last_match_at` and saves—i.e., validation has DB side effects and will run on any email change, not just account creation. However, the finding’s claim that “basic email format validation is silently dropped” isn’t verifiable as a regression from this diff, since the previous `email_validator` method also did not validate email format.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The BlockedEmails table has no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin controller, API, rake task, seed, or UI path creates records, so the entire blocklist feature is unreachable and unenforceable in practice. Operators cannot add a blocked email by any supported means; the shipped table, model, validator branch, and i18n string are dead weight until someone hand-inserts rows, and 'comprehensive email validation for blocked users' is not actually delivered to any user.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds the `blocked_emails` table/model and enforces it via `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), but within this diff there is no code path (controller/admin UI/API/seed/task) shown that creates or manages `BlockedEmail` records. That makes the feature operational only if operators insert rows by some out-of-band mechanism (e.g., console/SQL), which is a legitimate completeness/operability concern. However, it is not a verifiable correctness bug from the diff alone because enforcement does work when rows exist, and record-creation tooling could exist elsewhere outside this patch.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The signup error response now echoes user.errors.to_hash and the submitted name/username/email back to any anonymous client, untraceable to the stated blocked-email requirement. Unrelated scope expansion of a public unauthenticated endpoint: anonymous attackers can use the structured errors/values payload to enumerate which emails are on the blocklist (distinct 'blocked' message vs 'not_allowed' message) and to probe username/email uniqueness rules, with no requirement in this PR calling for it.

adjudication.rationale: In `UsersController#create`, the failure JSON response was expanded to include `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` for any unsuccessful signup. This is a public/unauthenticated endpoint and the new structured `errors` field makes validation outcomes machine-readable (e.g., uniqueness failures, and the new `EmailValidator` adds distinct messages for `user.email.not_allowed` vs `user.email.blocked`), facilitating automated probing/enumeration beyond what was previously returned as a single formatted `message` string. The added `values` echo is unnecessary for security and further broadens the response surface.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The rejectedEmails client-side mechanism is not traceable to a blocked-email requirement: it caches the email on ANY email validation failure and then suppresses revalidation with a generic 'invalid' message, conflating server-side blocking with generic client validation state. A user who fixes a typo elsewhere and resubmits the same blocked email gets the generic user.email.invalid message instead of the specific blocked/not_allowed reason the server returned, and the rejectedEmails array lives for the controller lifetime with no reset path, so a transient server error permanently marks an email invalid for the session; reviewers cannot tell from the diff which requirement this client state serves.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `rejectedEmails` to the create account controller and, once the server returns any `errors.email`, pushes `result.values.email` into that array. Thereafter, `emailValidation` short-circuits on `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and returns a generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` (not the specific server-provided reason like `user.email.not_allowed`/`user.email.blocked`), and the computed property depends on `rejectedEmails.@each`, so this persists for the controller lifetime with no reset shown. This is a concrete, diff-grounded UX/logic concern about conflating server-side reasons into a generic client-side invalid state, though it’s not clearly a hard functional break.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? mutates and saves statistics (match_count, last_match_at) from inside a read-path validator with no stated requirement for tracking, and the :do_nothing action still increments the counters and hits the DB on every check. Statistics churn is triggered by anyone probing signups (including with do_nothing records, giving attackers a write oracle), and a concurrent save under the unique-email constraint can raise out of validation, turning a signup check into a 500 — none of this behavior is demanded by the PR's stated intent.

[ADVISORY] The new validator's spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? entirely and only exercises the blocked branch, leaving the migrated whitelist/blacklist logic (previously exercised via User#email_validator) without any coverage in this diff. The relocation of domain restriction logic from app/models/user.rb into the validator class is behavior-bearing but unverifiable: a regression in email_in_restriction_setting? or the whitelist-takes-precedence branch ships undetected, and the domain logic is now duplicated in coverage obligation with no test owner.

adjudication.rationale: The diff moves domain whitelist/blacklist enforcement from User#email_validator (deleted in app/models/user.rb) into the new EmailValidator (lib/validators/email_validator.rb), including precedence (whitelist branch before blacklist) and regex matching via email_in_restriction_setting?. However, the added spec (spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb) only stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and asserts an error is/ isn’t present for that branch; it provides no coverage for the migrated whitelist/blacklist behavior or the precedence/regex logic. This is a concrete, diff-grounded test gap for newly relocated behavior rather than a functional defect proven by the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] should_block? performs a read-modify-write on match_count (record.match_count += 1; record.save) with no atomic increment or row lock, so concurrent signup attempts against the same blocked email lose counter updates. Two simultaneous requests both read match_count=N and both write N+1; the counter permanently undercounts, corrupting the stats the feature exists to collect. Fix is an atomic UPDATE blocked_emails SET match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ? WHERE email = ?

adjudication.rationale: In app/models/blocked_email.rb, BlockedEmail.should_block? does a non-atomic read-modify-write: `record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now; record.save`. Under concurrent requests for the same `email`, two threads/processes can both read the same match_count and both persist `N+1`, losing an increment and undercounting stats. The finding’s suggested atomic UPDATE (or increment_counter/locking) addresses this race.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] should_block? looks up the blocked email with an exact case-sensitive where(email: email), while email input casing is user-controlled, so 'Spam@x.com' misses a row stored as 'spam@x.com' and the block is bypassed. An attacker trivially defeats the blocklist by varying letter case, and admin-entered blocked emails silently fail to block; the write path (User#email validated downcased elsewhere) and this read path disagree on canonical form.

adjudication.rationale: BlockedEmail.should_block?(email) does an exact lookup (BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first) and the EmailValidator passes the raw value through. The model/migration add no canonicalization (e.g., downcasing) for BlockedEmail.email or for the validated value, so a case-variant like 'Spam@x.com' can fail to match a stored 'spam@x.com' depending on DB collation (e.g., PostgreSQL is case-sensitive), bypassing the intended block. The finding’s extra claim about User email being downcased elsewhere isn’t shown in this diff, but the case-sensitive lookup issue is grounded here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which performs a database write (match_count increment + save) inside model validation, so every email validation — not just account creation — mutates the blocked_emails table, and a failed save (e.g. concurrent unique-index violation) silently no-ops with no error handling. Validation becomes a hot write path: any code path that revalidates a user's email (admin edits, email change flows) bumps match_count even when no blocking decision was requested, inflating the metric; the concurrency-induced save failure is swallowed, also skipping the increment inconsistently.

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb, validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) whenever the attribute has no prior errors. BlockedEmail.should_block? (app/models/blocked_email.rb) performs a write on every match (increments match_count, sets last_match_at, and save), even when action_type is :do_nothing. This makes model validation a side-effecting/hot write path and can inflate match_count during any email revalidation (not just signup). However, the finding’s example of a concurrent unique-index violation on save isn’t supported by the diff because should_block? updates an existing row’s counters, not inserting a duplicate email.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The client records the rejected email verbatim from result.values.email and compares it with case-sensitive contains() against the raw accountEmail input, so server-normalized or case-varied retries (e.g. user retypes 'Bob@X.com' after 'bob@x.com' was rejected) bypass the client-side rejectedEmails fast path and re-submit to the server. The UX guard the diff adds only fires on exact-string re-entry; users get the full round-trip error again, and the rejectedEmails array grows unboundedly within the modal session with duplicate/case variants of the same address.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, the new fast-path checks `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` where `email` is the raw `accountEmail` string, and failures append `result.values.email` via `pushObject` without normalization or de-duplication. `Ember.Array#contains` on strings is exact/`===`, so the guard only prevents re-submission for exact-string re-entry; case/whitespace variants would not match, and repeated failures can grow `rejectedEmails` during the modal session (including duplicates). This is a UX/efficiency edge-case rather than a hard functional defect, since server-side validation still runs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The error response now echoes user.attributes.slice('name','username','email') and a raw errors hash back to the client, coupling the JSON contract to User column names with no versioning — any rename or reshaping of user attributes silently changes the public signup-failure payload the new client code depends on. Client and server now co-evolve on an undocumented envelope (result.errors.email / result.values.email); a server-side attribute rename breaks the client-side rejection tracking with no compile-time or contract signal.

adjudication.rationale: Diff adds a new signup failure payload shape in `UsersController#create`: `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`. The client change in `create_account_controller.js` explicitly depends on `result.errors.email` and `result.values.email` to track `rejectedEmails`. This creates a tight, undocumented coupling between server-side attribute/error key names (e.g., "email") and client logic; if the server renames/reshapes attributes or error serialization, the client-side rejection tracking can silently stop working. This is a contract/maintainability issue introduced by the change, not an immediate functional defect in the diff itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] action_type is stored as a bare integer backed by an in-code Enum with no CHECK constraint or lookup semantics, and the table hardcodes a per-email block model — extending to per-domain or per-pattern blocking (the natural next step for a blocklist) requires a schema migration rather than a data change. Admins must add one row per exact email address; the magic integer column admits any value outside the Enum's two actions, and the schema shape bakes in the exact-match single-address rule.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `blocked_emails.action_type` as an unconstrained integer column (migration: `t.integer :action_type, null: false`) and models it via an in-code `Enum` (`BlockedEmail.actions`), with runtime comparison `record.action_type == actions[:block]` in `BlockedEmail.should_block?`. There is no DB-level CHECK/foreign key/lookup table to prevent out-of-range integers, so invalid values are possible. The schema and query logic also hardcode exact-email matching only (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` and `t.string :email`), so supporting domain/pattern blocking would require schema/logic changes rather than just data changes. This is a valid design/extension concern, not a directly verifiable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? compares emails with exact case-sensitive equality and no normalization, so a blocked address is bypassed by any case variant or surrounding whitespace. An admin blocks 'spam@spamclub.com'; a registrant signs up with 'SPAM@spamclub.com' and User.where email lookup misses the record, so the block silently does not apply — the feature's core intent (block a specific email) fails for trivially mutated input. The uniqueness validation on User is likewise default (case-sensitive here), so the drift between 'blocked' and 'enforced' widens.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` performs `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` (app/models/blocked_email.rb) with no `strip`/`downcase` normalization, and the new `EmailValidator` passes the raw `value` through to `should_block?` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). The BlockedEmail model only validates uniqueness with default settings (case-sensitivity depends on DB/collation and is not forced here), and `User` email uniqueness was changed to `validates :email, ... uniqueness: true` without `case_sensitive: false`. From what’s shown, a blocked address can plausibly be bypassed by trivial casing/whitespace variants because matching is exact and unnormalized, which undermines the intended “block a specific email” behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Once an email is pushed into rejectedEmails, the client-side emailValid computation permanently reports 'invalid' for that address for the rest of the modal session, with no mechanism to re-check against the server. If the operator removes the block (or the first failure was transient), the user cannot re-submit the same address without closing and reopening the dialog; submitDisabled keeps the form disabled based on a cached server verdict that is never refreshed — the feedback shown ('invalid') also contradicts the actual server reason ('blocked'), which is a second drift between the server's error taxonomy and the client's displayed message.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, `emailValid` now hard-fails if `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and returns reason `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` (lines added around `if (this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email))`). On a failed create, the controller pushes the attempted email into `rejectedEmails` whenever `result.errors.email` is present (`pushObject(result.values.email)`). There is no code in the diff to ever remove/expire entries or to re-check the same email against the server; additionally `emailValid` is recomputed on `rejectedEmails.@each`, making the “invalid” state persist for that address for the remainder of the modal session. This can prevent a user from retrying the same email after conditions change, and it also discards the server’s more specific error taxonomy (e.g., `user.email.blocked`/`not_allowed`) by always showing `user.email.invalid` for cached rejections.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] should_block? increments match_count and writes to the database during model validation, and does so under a read-modify-write race with no locking or atomic update. Every concurrent signup attempt with a blocked email does SELECT then UPDATE; concurrent requests lose increments (match_count undercounts) and, more importantly, user validation now performs a write side effect — a validation pass can fail with a DB error on a record being validated for an unrelated reason, turning a pure check into a mutating operation. An unauthenticated user can also drive writes to blocked_emails on every signup attempt, making the table a write-amplification target.
matched_golden_ids: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags that should_block?/should_block_email? performs a write (incrementing match_count/updating DB) during what should be a read/check operation, making the method/validation impure and misleading. It also explicitly calls out concurrent read-modify-write race conditions and side effects causing potential failures, matching the golden issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? is an instance-lookup plus mutation helper implemented as a class method with a hidden write side effect, and record.save's return value is ignored. The next maintainer calling should_block? in any read context (admin UI preview, API serialization) silently mutates statistics; a save failure (validation/DB) is swallowed, so match data silently diverges from real attempts. Staff-level concern: this couples 'is it blocked' with 'record the hit' and will be reused incorrectly.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` (app/models/blocked_email.rb) performs a lookup and then mutates/persists `match_count` and `last_match_at` via `record.save` before returning the boolean block decision. The method name/signature reads like a pure predicate, but it has a hidden write side effect, so reusing it in any “read” context would silently change data. Also, the return value of `record.save` is ignored, so persistence failures would not be surfaced and statistics could silently diverge. This is a concrete, diff-grounded design/architecture concern rather than a directly verifiable functional bug in the shown call site (EmailValidator).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked-email check is only reached when the domain whitelist/blacklist checks produce no errors, and the validator runs only if: :email_changed? — blocked-list enforcement is skipped for existing users whose email is unchanged on save and silently bypassed whenever a domain rule already errors. Behavioral asymmetry: a blocked email that also matches the blacklist gets the 'not_allowed' message instead of the blocked one (harmless), but the if: :email_changed? gating means the block list is never consulted for existing accounts, so an admin block only affects new signups/changes — an unstated narrowing of the feature's intent that no test covers.

adjudication.rationale: Diff shows the new blocked-email enforcement lives inside `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?` only runs when `record.errors[attribute].blank?`) and the `User` model invokes it only `if: :email_changed?` (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`). This means (1) blocked-email checking is skipped on saves where the email is unchanged, and (2) if a whitelist/blacklist rule already adds an error, the blocked-email check is not reached, so the user sees `not_allowed` instead of `blocked`. Whether this is a defect depends on intended scope, but it is a concrete behavioral limitation introduced by placing the block check behind the same gate and error-short-circuit, and there’s no test covering the “existing user unchanged email” case.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The only spec for the new validator stubs out BlockedEmail.should_block? entirely, so the integration path actually shipped in User (email: true validator wired against SiteSetting whitelist/blacklist plus the real BlockedEmail lookup) is untested. The domain-whitelist/blacklist behavior moved from User#email_validator into EmailValidator is exercised by zero tests in this diff; a regression in the copied gsub/regexp logic or the should_block? integration would pass CI. The stubbed tests also assert only on the stub, verifying nothing about validate_each's real logic.

adjudication.rationale: Diff introduces `EmailValidator` with domain whitelist/blacklist logic plus a real `BlockedEmail.should_block?` lookup (`lib/validators/email_validator.rb`). The only new validator spec (`spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb`) stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` in both examples and does not exercise the whitelist/blacklist branches at all. While `BlockedEmail` itself has its own model spec, the validator’s integration behavior (calling the real `BlockedEmail.should_block?` after ensuring no prior errors, and the copied regexp restriction logic) is not covered by any test shown in this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The client keys off result.errors.email truthiness but pushes result.values.email; if the server returns errors without a values payload (older API responses, plugin-rendered errors) the pushObject silently stores undefined. rejectedEmails gains an undefined entry; Em.A.contains(undefined) then never matches a real email, so this is latent today but breaks the moment another server error path includes errors.email without values — a producer/consumer contract split across files with no shared definition of the payload shape.

adjudication.rationale: In the client failure path, the diff adds `if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values) { ... pushObject(result.values.email); }`. The guard prevents pushing when `values` is entirely absent, but it does not ensure `result.values.email` is present, so it could push `undefined` if some server/error path returns `values` without an `email` key. The current server change includes `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`, so it works for this path, but the producer/consumer contract is implicit and brittle across files; tightening the check to `result.values && result.values.email` (or using the submitted email) would make it robust.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The whitelist/blacklist regex `@(#{domains})` is unanchored, so an email like `attacker@good.com.evil.com` matches the whitelist entry `good.com` and passes the whitelist check while actually resolving at the attacker-controlled domain `evil.com`. An attacker registers with a whitelist-spoofing domain address, defeating the admin's email-domain restriction (the same unanchored match also lets blacklist bypasses like a subdomain-free variant be engineered); the old User#email_in_restriction_setting? carried the same flaw but this diff re-commits it in the new validator that now governs all email changes.
matched_golden_ids: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both identify the same underlying flaw: the `@(#{domains})` regex is not properly anchored/bounded, so it can match a whitelisted domain as a substring/suffix within a longer attacker-controlled domain (e.g., `good.com.evil.com` or `evil.example.com`), allowing whitelist bypass (and related blacklist issues).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] should_block? performs an exact-match `where(email: email)` lookup with no case normalization, so `Block@SpamFromHome.org` or any mixed-case variant of a blocked address is not found and is not blocked. Unless every caller downcases before validation (no normalization is added anywhere in this diff), an attacker registers with a case-variant of any blocked email, defeating the block list; the match_count statistic also silently diverges across case variants.

adjudication.rationale: In the added blocking path, `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` does an exact `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` lookup (new `app/models/blocked_email.rb`) and `EmailValidator` passes the raw `value` through without any downcasing/normalization (new `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`). The client-side caching of rejections also uses exact string matching (`rejectedEmails.contains(email)` in `create_account_controller.js`). With no case normalization shown anywhere in this diff, a case-variant like `Block@SpamFromHome.org` would not match a stored `block@spamfromhome.org`, bypassing blocking and splitting `match_count` across variants.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The signup failure response now echoes `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values` including the submitted email, turning the unauthenticated /users endpoint into an oracle for probing the admin's blocked-email list and distinguishing 'blocked email' rejections from other validation failures. An unauthenticated attacker can enumerate which specific email addresses the site operators have blocked (and confirm whether a given address was the reason a signup failed), leaking moderation configuration that was previously not exposed per-address.

adjudication.rationale: In `UsersController#create`, the failure JSON response now includes `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`. The diff also introduces `BlockedEmail` and an `EmailValidator` that adds a distinct `user.email.blocked` error when `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` is true. Together, this makes the unauthenticated signup endpoint a reliable oracle: an attacker can submit arbitrary emails and directly observe whether the rejection is specifically due to being blocked (via `errors["email"]` containing the blocked message) versus other validation failures, thereby probing the blocked-email configuration per address. The echoed `values.email` additionally confirms the probed email in the response.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? performs a read-modify-write (`match_count += 1` then `save`) inside the signup validation path with no locking or uniqueness retry, and it fires for every signup attempt with a matching address. Concurrent signup attempts with a blocked email race on the counter update (lost updates), and an unauthenticated attacker can drive unbounded writes to the blocked_emails row by repeatedly submitting the blocked address; under contention the `record.save` can also raise and abort the signup with a 500 instead of a clean validation error.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (app/models/blocked_email.rb) which does a non-atomic read-modify-write (`record.match_count += 1; record.save`) on every signup validation where the email matches (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). This can cause lost updates under concurrent requests and creates a write-amplification/DoS risk since unauthenticated signup attempts will repeatedly update the same row. However, the core correctness of blocking is based on `action_type` (not the counter), and `record.save` (non-bang) typically won’t raise; a guaranteed 500 on contention isn’t verifiable from the diff. So it’s a real, diff-grounded concern (performance/availability/statistics integrity), but not a clearly user-visible correctness defect in the main feature.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table is created but this diff ships no writer anywhere (no admin UI, API, rake task, or seed path), so the block list cannot be populated or its action_type toggled by operators. Operators cannot actually use the feature this PR adds: BlockedEmail rows stay empty and should_block? always returns false, making the shipped validator branch and client-side rejectedEmails machinery inert until a separate admin surface lands.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `BlockedEmail` model + migration and wires it into `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), plus client-side caching of rejected emails, but it does not add any way (controller/admin UI/API/seed/rake task) to create or manage `blocked_emails` rows. From what’s shown, operators can’t populate or toggle `action_type` through the app, so the feature is operationally incomplete even though the code paths exist.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Both tests stub BlockedEmail.should_block? with canned return values, so the spec exercises only the validator's if-branch against a mock and never the real BlockedEmail lookup the feature depends on. A regression in BlockedEmail.should_block? (e.g. the record.save failure path, the action_type comparison, or the where(email:) lookup being broken by casing/collation) leaves both tests green because should_block? is stubbed false/true and the real model code is never run inside validation; the spec gives false confidence that blocked emails are actually rejected end-to-end.

adjudication.rationale: In spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb both examples stub BlockedEmail.should_block? to true/false, so that spec verifies only that the validator adds an error based on the return value, not that a real BlockedEmail row causes validation to fail. Although there is separate coverage of BlockedEmail.should_block? in spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb, the validator spec as written would not catch integration issues (e.g., passing a differently-cased email, lookup quirks) because the DB lookup path is mocked out.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The domain whitelist/blacklist logic relocated from app/models/user.rb into lib/validators/email_validator.rb has zero test coverage in this diff — the spec only covers the blocked-email branch and never asserts that a whitelist/blacklist violation adds the 'not_allowed' error. The most error-prone code in the moved block (the '.'->'\.' gsub and case-insensitive Regexp.new construction) is unverified: a typo or regexp regression silently disables or inverts domain restriction, and no test in this diff fails. Checked spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb, spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb — neither touches the restriction-setting path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff moves the domain whitelist/blacklist restriction logic into `lib/validators/email_validator.rb` (checks `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist/blacklist`, builds a case-insensitive `Regexp` after `gsub('.', '\.')`, and adds `user.email.not_allowed`). The added spec `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` only stubs and asserts the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` branch and never sets `SiteSetting` or asserts `not_allowed` errors for whitelist/blacklist violations. No other added/modified spec in the diff covers those paths, so the finding about zero test coverage for the relocated restriction logic is accurate and diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The test named "doesn't add an error when email doesn't match a blocked email" tests the negative case via a stub rather than a real non-blocked record, mirroring the implementation's branch instead of the spec (stub false → assert no error is the trivially-true half of the branch). The test cannot detect a regression where the validator adds a 'blocked' error even when should_block? returns false (e.g. a misplaced errors.add outside the if) — the assertion holds only because the stub path happens to skip the add; a data-driven case (a real BlockedEmail row with action_type :do_nothing) would catch both this validator branch and the real lookup at once.

adjudication.rationale: In `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb`, the negative-case example stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` to return `false` and then asserts no error. This means the validator spec does not exercise the real `BlockedEmail.should_block?` lookup/statistics path (i.e., it’s not an end-to-end/data-driven negative case). However, the finding overstates that this test “cannot detect” a regression where `errors.add` happens regardless of `should_block?`; if `errors.add` were unconditionally executed, this test would fail. The core, diff-grounded issue is limited to test coverage/integration depth, not a functional bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The migration enforces action_type NOT NULL with no DEFAULT, while the default lives only in the BlockedEmail model's before_validation callback, so any row created outside the AR model (seed, admin console, future backfill SQL) raises a NOT NULL violation. Operators seeding or mass-inserting blocked emails via SQL/console get an insert failure on action_type; the schema-level contract diverges from the model-level default.

adjudication.rationale: In the migration `CreateBlockedEmails`, `action_type` is declared `null: false` with no DB default (`t.integer :action_type, null: false`), while the only defaulting behavior is in the Rails model callback `BlockedEmail#set_defaults` (`self.action_type ||= BlockedEmail.actions[:block]`). This means inserts that bypass the AR model (raw SQL, some bulk loaders, manual scripts) and omit `action_type` will fail at the DB level, creating a schema/model contract mismatch. This is a concrete, diff-grounded maintainability/operability issue, but not an in-app correctness bug since AR-created rows will get the default.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? performs a state-mutating write (match_count increment + last_match_at update) inside the email validation path and ignores the result of record.save, so failed stat writes are silently swallowed. Every signup attempt with a changed email triggers an UPDATE on blocked_emails from an unauthenticated request path; if the save fails (validation or contention) the match statistic is silently lost with no log, and because validation now has a side effect, retrying a signup that fails some other validation double-increments match_count, so the admin-facing statistic counts validation attempts, not actually blocked registrations.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the method mutates state (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`) and calls `record.save` without checking/handling failure (`app/models/blocked_email.rb`). This is invoked from the email validation path (`lib/validators/email_validator.rb`), so validation now has a side effect and repeated validations (e.g., retrying signup after failing other validations) will increment `match_count` again, meaning the statistic counts validation hits rather than only successful blocked registrations. While this doesn’t break the core blocking decision (it returns based on `action_type` regardless of save success), it is a diff-grounded design/observability concern and can silently lose stats on failed saves.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] match_count is updated via read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1 then save) rather than an atomic increment, so concurrent signups interleave and lose increments. Two simultaneous registrations matching the same blocked email both read the same match_count and one UPDATE overwrites the other, permanently undercounting matches; the correct `increment_counter`/`update_column(match_count: match_count + 1)` form was available.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the code does `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save` (read-modify-write). Under concurrent calls for the same `blocked_emails.email`, two processes can read the same `match_count` and both write back the same incremented value, losing one increment and undercounting matches. This is directly shown in the diff and would be avoided by an atomic DB increment (e.g., `increment_counter`/`update_all`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked-email lookup `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` is an exact case-sensitive match while the domain blacklist/whitelist regexp in the same validator is case-insensitive, so case variants of a blocked address silently pass the block. An admin blocks 'spam@foo.com' but a registrant signing up as 'Spam@foo.com' or 'SPAM@FOO.COM' is not blocked and account creation succeeds, defeating the feature for the trivially reachable case-variant bypass.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` the lookup is `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, which is an exact equality match and (in common DBs like Postgres) case-sensitive. The validator’s domain restriction regex is explicitly case-insensitive (`Regexp.new(..., true)`), so a blocked address like `spam@foo.com` would not be found for `Spam@foo.com`/`SPAM@FOO.COM`, allowing a trivial bypass of the new blocked-email feature. The diff shows no normalization (e.g., downcasing) or case-insensitive query/index to prevent this.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The client pushes the email into rejectedEmails whenever any result.errors.email is present, including 'has already been taken', and email_valid then renders the generic 'invalid' message for an email that is actually taken. A user whose email fails uniqueness sees the inline validation claim the address is invalid while the real reason (taken) is only in the transient flash, misdirecting debugging and user comprehension; the rejectedEmails list is also never cleared on success or modal reopen, so the stale entry persists for the controller's lifetime.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, on failed create the client pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` whenever `result.errors.email` exists (no filtering by error type) (lines adding `pushObject(result.values.email)`). Then `emailValidation` immediately treats any email in `rejectedEmails` as `failed: true` with reason `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` (new early return), regardless of whether the actual server-side email error was e.g. uniqueness (“has already been taken”). This makes the inline validation message incorrect for some real server error cases introduced by the diff.
